claim: Classic supervised learning models posit that when two stimuli predict similar outcomes, their representations should integrate.
source: Classic supervised learning models posit that, when two stimuli predict similar outcomes, their representations should integrate.
evidence: This is a statement about what classic supervised learning models predict, supported by citations to foundational work in the field.

claim: Pairing two stimuli with a shared associate can sometimes cause differentiation, depending on the parameters of the study and the brain region being examined.
source: However, these models have recently been challenged by studies showing that pairing two stimuli with a shared associate can sometimes cause differentiation, depending on the parameters of the study and the brain region being examined.
evidence: This claim is supported by references to recent empirical studies that challenge supervised learning models.

claim: The model can exhibit integration or differentiation depending on the amount of activity allowed to spread to competitors.
source: The model can exhibit integration or differentiation depending on the amount of activity allowed to spread to competitors — inactive memories are not modified, connections to moderately active competitors are weakened (leading to differentiation), and connections to highly active competitors are strengthened (leading to integration).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the model's behavior based on the computational simulations presented in the manuscript.

claim: When differentiation occurs as a result of this unsupervised learning mechanism, it will be rapid and asymmetric.
source: The model also makes several novel predictions — most importantly, that when differentiation occurs as a result of this unsupervised learning mechanism, it will be rapid and asymmetric, and it will give rise to anticorrelated representations in the region of the brain that is the source of the differentiation.
evidence: This is a prediction derived from the model's behavior in simulations.

claim: Differentiation driven by the NMPH will give rise to anticorrelated representations in the region of the brain that is the source of the differentiation.
source: The model also makes several novel predictions — most importantly, that when differentiation occurs as a result of this unsupervised learning mechanism, it will be rapid and asymmetric, and it will give rise to anticorrelated representations in the region of the brain that is the source of the differentiation.
evidence: This is a prediction derived from the model's behavior in simulations.

claim: Numerous fMRI studies have obtained evidence supporting supervised learning theories by utilizing representational similarity analysis to track how patterns evoked by similar stimuli change over time.
source: Numerous fMRI studies have obtained evidence supporting these theories, by utilizing representational similarity analysis to track how the patterns evoked by similar stimuli change over time (e.g. Schapiro et al., 2013; Schapiro et al., 2016; Tompary and Davachi, 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to specific fMRI studies.

claim: Linking stimuli to shared associates can lead to differentiation rather than integration in the hippocampus.
source: However, other studies have found that linking stimuli to shared associates can lead to differentiation rather than integration. For instance, in one fMRI study, differentiation was observed in the hippocampus when participants were tasked with predicting the same face in response to two similar scenes (i.e. two barns), so much so that the two scenes became less neurally similar to each other than they were to unrelated stimuli (Favila et al., 2016; for related findings, see Schlichting et al., 2015; Molitor et al., 2021; for reviews, see Brunec et al., 2020; Duncan and Schlichting, 2018; Ritvo et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to empirical fMRI studies.

claim: In Favila et al., 2016, two similar scenes became less neurally similar to each other than they were to unrelated stimuli when linked to the same face.
source: For instance, in one fMRI study, differentiation was observed in the hippocampus when participants were tasked with predicting the same face in response to two similar scenes (i.e. two barns), so much so that the two scenes became less neurally similar to each other than they were to unrelated stimuli (Favila et al., 2016; for related findings, see Schlichting et al., 2015; Molitor et al., 2021; for reviews, see Brunec et al., 2020; Duncan and Schlichting, 2018; Ritvo et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a specific empirical finding from Favila et al., 2016.

claim: Supervised learning models predict that connection weights underlying memories should be adjusted to make them more similar to each other when stimuli share a common associate.
source: Findings of this sort present a challenge to supervised learning models, which predict that the connection weights underlying these memories should be adjusted to make them more (not less) similar to each other.
evidence: This is a statement about what supervised learning models predict, based on established knowledge of these models.

claim: Similarity reversal, whereby stimuli that have more features in common show less hippocampal pattern similarity, has been observed in a wide range of studies.
source: This kind of 'similarity reversal', whereby stimuli that have more features in common (or share a common associate) show less hippocampal pattern similarity, has now been observed in a wide range of studies (e.g. Favila et al., 2016; Schlichting et al., 2015; Molitor et al., 2021; Chanales et al., 2017; Dimsdale-Zucker et al., 2018; Wanjia et al., 2021; Zeithamova et al., 2018; Jiang et al., 2020; Fernandez et al., 2023; Wammes et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple empirical studies.

claim: The Bienenstock-Cooper-Munro (BCM) learning rule is the most well-known learning algorithm with a U-shaped relationship between neural activity and synaptic weight change.
source: We previously argued (Ritvo et al., 2019) that learning algorithms positing a U-shaped relationship between neural activity and synaptic weight change — where low levels of activity at retrieval lead to no change, moderate levels of activity lead to synaptic weakening, and high levels of activity lead to synaptic strengthening — may be able to account for these results; the Bienenstock-Cooper-Munro (BCM) learning rule (Bienenstock et al., 1982; Cooper, 2004) is the most well-known learning algorithm with this property, but other algorithms with this property have also been proposed (Norman et al., 2006; Diederich and Opper, 1987).
evidence: This is a statement about the BCM learning rule supported by citations.

claim: If competitor activity is low while retrieving a target memory, the NMPH predicts no representational change.
source: If the activity of a competing memory is low while retrieving a target memory (Figure 1C), the NMPH predicts no representational change.
evidence: This is a prediction from the NMPH model, illustrated in Figure 1C.

claim: If competitor activity is moderate, the NMPH predicts that connections to shared units will be weakened, leading to differentiation.
source: If competitor activity is moderate (Figure 1B), the connections to the shared units will be weakened, leading to differentiation.
evidence: This is a prediction from the NMPH model, illustrated in Figure 1B.

claim: If competitor activity is high, the NMPH predicts that connections to shared units will be strengthened, leading to integration.
source: If competitor activity is high (Figure 1A), the connections to the shared units will be strengthened, leading to integration.
evidence: This is a prediction from the NMPH model, illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: The model was constructed to use only unsupervised, U-shaped learning and not supervised learning.
source: The model was constructed such that it only used unsupervised, U-shaped learning and not supervised learning.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the model's construction.

claim: Unsupervised, U-shaped learning is viewed as a supplementary tool the brain uses to reduce interference of competitors, not a replacement for error-driven learning.
source: Importantly, we do not think that unsupervised, U-shaped learning function is a replacement for error-driven learning; instead, we view it as a supplementary tool the brain uses to reduce interference of competitors (Ritvo et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a statement about the authors' theoretical perspective, supported by a citation.

claim: The model was built using the Emergent simulation framework.
source: The model was built using the Emergent simulation framework (Aisa et al., 2008).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the computational tools used, supported by a citation.

claim: The model includes four layers: category, item, hidden, and output.
source: With those points in mind, we built the model to include four layers: category, item, hidden, and output.
evidence: This is a direct description of the model architecture.

claim: The category and item layers are bidirectionally connected to the hidden layer.
source: In all models, the category and item layers are bidirectionally connected to the hidden layer; the hidden layer is bidirectionally connected to the output layer; and the hidden layer also has recurrent connections back to itself.
evidence: This is a direct description of the model architecture.

claim: The hidden layer is bidirectionally connected to the output layer.
source: In all models, the category and item layers are bidirectionally connected to the hidden layer; the hidden layer is bidirectionally connected to the output layer; and the hidden layer also has recurrent connections back to itself.
evidence: This is a direct description of the model architecture.

claim: The hidden layer has recurrent connections back to itself.
source: In all models, the category and item layers are bidirectionally connected to the hidden layer; the hidden layer is bidirectionally connected to the output layer; and the hidden layer also has recurrent connections back to itself.
evidence: This is a direct description of the model architecture.

claim: All connections in the model are modifiable through learning.
source: All of these connections are modifiable through learning.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the model's learning mechanism.

claim: Inhibitory oscillations allow activity to spread to competitors.
source: The main method we use to allow activity to spread to the competitor is through inhibitory oscillations.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the model's mechanism for competitor activation.

claim: Prior work has argued that inhibitory oscillations could play a key role in competition-dependent learning.
source: Prior work has argued that inhibitory oscillations could play a key role in this kind of competition-dependent learning (Norman et al., 2006; Norman et al., 2007; Singh et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior theoretical work.

claim: The model implements oscillations through a sinusoidal function which lowers and raises inhibition over the course of the trial.
source: Our model implements oscillations through a sinusoidal function which lowers and raises inhibition over the course of the trial, allowing competitors to 'pop up' when inhibition is lower.
evidence: This is a direct description of the model's implementation.

claim: In Chanales et al., 2021, when color similarity was low (48° difference), participants recalled colors accurately.
source: Chanales et al., 2021 found that, for low levels of pairmate color similarity (i.e. 72° and 48° color difference), participants were able to recall the colors accurately when cued with a face and an object.
evidence: This is a specific empirical finding from Chanales et al., 2021.

claim: In Chanales et al., 2021, when color similarity was increased to 24° difference, color reports were biased away from the pairmate, leading to a repulsion effect.
source: However, when color similarity was increased (i.e. 24° color difference), the color reports were biased away from the pairmate, leading to a repulsion effect.
evidence: This is a specific empirical finding from Chanales et al., 2021.

claim: In Chanales et al., 2021, when color similarity was increased to 6° difference, the repulsion effects were eliminated.
source: When the color similarity was increased even further (i.e. 6° color difference), the repulsion effects were eliminated (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is a specific empirical finding from Chanales et al., 2021, illustrated in Figure 3B.

claim: The model qualitatively replicates the key pattern of results in Chanales et al., 2021, whereby increasing color similarity led to a repulsion effect in color recall, which went away as similarity increased further.
source: In summary, this version of our model qualitatively replicates the key pattern of results in Chanales et al., 2021, whereby increasing color similarity led to a repulsion effect in color recall, which went away as similarity increased further.
evidence: This is a summary statement about the model's ability to replicate empirical findings.

claim: In the model of Chanales et al., 2021, the repulsion effect in the 2/6 condition is asymmetric: one pairmate anchors in place and the other pairmate shifts its color representation.
source: A striking feature of the model is that the repulsion effect in the 2/6 condition is asymmetric: One pairmate anchors in place and the other pairmate shifts its color representation.
evidence: This is a finding from the model simulations, illustrated in Figure 4B.

claim: In the model, differentiation requires a high learning rate.
source: We found that differentiation requires a high learning rate.
evidence: This is a finding from the model simulations, illustrated in Figure 6A.

claim: In the model, when differentiation occurs, it happens abruptly.
source: A corollary of the fact that differentiation requires a high learning rate is that, when it does happen in the model, it happens abruptly.
evidence: This is an inference from the model's behavior, illustrated in Figure 6B.

claim: In the model, pairs of items that differentiate show anticorrelated representations.
source: Figure 6B also highlights that, for learning rates where robust differentiation effects occur in aggregate (i.e. there is a reduction in mean pattern similarity, averaging across model runs), these aggregate effects involve a bimodal distribution across model runs: For some model runs, learning processes give rise to anticorrelated representations, and for other model runs the model shows integration; this variance across model runs is attributable to random differences in the initial weight configuration of the model and/or in the order of item presentations across training epochs.
evidence: This is a finding from the model simulations, illustrated in Figure 6B.

claim: In Favila et al., 2016, participants learned scene-face associations where scenes were made up of highly similar pairs.
source: In this study (Figure 7A), participants were instructed to learn scene-face associations. Later, during the repeated face-test task, participants were shown a scene and asked to pick the correct face from a bank of faces. Scenes were made up of highly similar pairs (e.g. two bridges, two barns).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental design from Favila et al., 2016.

claim: In Favila et al., 2016, when two scenes predicted different faces, hippocampal representations for each scene were relatively orthogonalized.
source: When the two scenes predicted different faces, the hippocampal representations for each scene were relatively orthogonalized — hippocampal representations of the two pairmate scenes were just as similar to each other as to non-pairmate scenes.
evidence: This is a specific empirical finding from Favila et al., 2016.

claim: In Favila et al., 2016, when two scenes predicted the same face, differentiation resulted such that hippocampal representations of the two pairmate scenes were less similar to each other than to non-pairmate scenes.
source: However, when the two scenes predicted the same face, differentiation resulted, such that the hippocampal representations of the two pairmate scenes were less similar to each other than to non-pairmate scenes (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is a specific empirical finding from Favila et al., 2016, illustrated in Figure 7B.

claim: The model can account for the results of Favila et al., 2016, where learning about stimuli that share a paired associate can lead to differentiation.
source: This simulation demonstrates that the NMPH can explain the results of Favila et al., 2016, where learning about stimuli that share a paired associate can lead to differentiation.
evidence: This is a summary statement about the model's ability to replicate empirical findings.

claim: In Schlichting et al., 2015, participants learned to link novel objects with a common associate (AX and BX), sometimes in a blocked fashion and sometimes in an interleaved fashion.
source: This study examined how the learning curriculum affects representational change in different brain regions. Participants learned to link novel objects with a common associate (i.e. AX and BX). Sometimes these associates were presented in a blocked fashion (all AX before any BX) and sometimes they were presented in an interleaved fashion (Figure 9A).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental design from Schlichting et al., 2015.

claim: In Schlichting et al., 2015, some brain regions (e.g. right posterior hippocampus) showed differentiation for both blocked and interleaved conditions.
source: Some brain regions (e.g. right posterior hippocampus) showed differentiation for both blocked and interleaved conditions, some regions (e.g. left mPFC) showed integration for both conditions, and others (e.g. right anterior hippocampus) showed integration in the blocked condition but differentiation in the interleaved condition (Figure 9B).
evidence: This is a specific empirical finding from Schlichting et al., 2015, illustrated in Figure 9B.

claim: In Schlichting et al., 2015, some brain regions (e.g. left mPFC) showed integration for both blocked and interleaved conditions.
source: Some brain regions (e.g. right posterior hippocampus) showed differentiation for both blocked and interleaved conditions, some regions (e.g. left mPFC) showed integration for both conditions, and others (e.g. right anterior hippocampus) showed integration in the blocked condition but differentiation in the interleaved condition (Figure 9B).
evidence: This is a specific empirical finding from Schlichting et al., 2015, illustrated in Figure 9B.

claim: In Schlichting et al., 2015, some brain regions (e.g. right anterior hippocampus) showed integration in the blocked condition but differentiation in the interleaved condition.
source: Some brain regions (e.g. right posterior hippocampus) showed differentiation for both blocked and interleaved conditions, some regions (e.g. left mPFC) showed integration for both conditions, and others (e.g. right anterior hippocampus) showed integration in the blocked condition but differentiation in the interleaved condition (Figure 9B).
evidence: This is a specific empirical finding from Schlichting et al., 2015, illustrated in Figure 9B.

claim: In the model of Schlichting et al., 2015, the interleaved condition leads to differentiation whereas the blocked condition leads to integration.
source: Examining the correlation between the hidden-layer representations of A and B, we found that the interleaved condition leads to differentiation (see Video 8) whereas the blocked condition (where the AX connection is stronger) leads to integration (see Video 9; Figure 10A).
evidence: This is a finding from the model simulations, illustrated in Figure 10A.

claim: The model predicts that differentiation will be more evident in the hippocampus than in neocortex, insofar as hippocampus is thought to have a higher learning rate than neocortex.
source: Our finding that differentiation requires a high learning rate suggests that differentiation will be more evident in the hippocampus than in neocortex, insofar as hippocampus is thought to have a higher learning rate than neocortex (McClelland et al., 1995).
evidence: This is a prediction derived from the model's behavior, supported by a citation about hippocampal learning rates.

claim: Numerous studies have found differentiation effects in hippocampus but not in neocortical regions involved in sensory processing.
source: In keeping with this prediction, numerous studies have found differentiation effects in hippocampus but not in neocortical regions involved in sensory processing (e.g. Chanales et al., 2017; Favila et al., 2016; Zeithamova et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to empirical studies.

claim: Some studies have found differentiation effects in neocortex.
source: At the same time, some studies have found differentiation effects in neocortex (e.g. Schlichting et al., 2015; Wammes et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to empirical studies.

claim: Within the hippocampus, subregions with sparser activity (e.g. dentate gyrus, and to a lesser extent, CA3) will be more prone to differentiation.
source: Thus, within the hippocampus, subregions with sparser activity (e.g. dentate gyrus, and to a lesser extent, CA3; Barnes et al., 1990; GoodSmith et al., 2017; West et al., 1991) will be more prone to differentiation.
evidence: This is a prediction derived from the model's behavior, supported by citations about hippocampal subregion activity patterns.

claim: Wammes et al., 2022 manipulated the similarity of stimuli in a statistical learning experiment and found that moderate levels of visual similarity were associated with significant differentiation in the dentate gyrus but not other subregions.
source: For example, Wammes et al., 2022 manipulated the similarity of stimuli in a statistical learning experiment and found that moderate levels of visual similarity were associated with significant differentiation in the dentate gyrus but not other subregions.
evidence: This is a specific empirical finding from Wammes et al., 2022.

claim: Numerous studies have found greater differentiation in dentate gyrus / CA3 than in CA1.
source: Also, numerous studies have found greater differentiation in dentate gyrus / CA3 than in CA1 (e.g. Dimsdale-Zucker et al., 2018; Wanjia et al., 2021; Molitor et al., 2021; Kim et al., 2017; but see Zheng et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple empirical studies.

claim: Wanjia et al., 2021 identified the moment when participants were first able to confidently recall the correct associates linked to pairmates and found that differentiation was not evident before this point but was clearly evident after.
source: Wanjia et al., 2021 did exactly this: They identified the moment when participants were first able to confidently recall the correct associates that had been linked to a set of pairmates (visually similar scenes, as in Favila et al., 2016), and then looked before and after that moment at the neural similarity of the pairmates. As predicted by our model, differentiation was not evident before this point, and it was clearly evident after this point.
evidence: This is a specific empirical finding from Wanjia et al., 2021 that supports the model's predictions.

claim: Multiple neurophysiological studies have found that moderate postsynaptic depolarization leads to synaptic weakening and higher levels of depolarization lead to synaptic strengthening.
source: In brief, there are three lines of work that support the U shape: First, multiple neurophysiological studies have found that moderate postsynaptic depolarization leads to synaptic weakening and higher levels of depolarization lead to synaptic strengthening (e.g. Artola et al., 1990; Hansel, 1996).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to neurophysiological studies.

claim: Several human neuroscience studies using pattern classifiers applied to fMRI and EEG data have found that low levels of memory activation lead to no change in memory strength, moderate levels lead to impaired subsequent memory, and higher levels lead to increased subsequent memory.
source: Second, human neuroscience studies have used pattern classifiers, applied to fMRI and EEG data, to measure memory activation, and have related this measure to subsequent memory accessibility; several studies using this approach have found that low levels of activation lead to no change in memory strength, moderate levels of activation lead to impaired subsequent memory, and higher levels of activation lead to increased subsequent memory (e.g. Newman and Norman, 2010; Detre et al., 2013; Kim et al., 2014; for related findings, see Lewis-Peacock and Norman, 2014; Wang et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to human neuroscience studies.

claim: Wammes et al., 2022 manipulated memory activation by varying the visual similarity of pairmates and observed a U-shaped function relating visual similarity to representational change in the hippocampus.
source: Third, a recent human fMRI study by Wammes et al., 2022 manipulated memory activation by varying the visual similarity of pairmates and observed a U-shaped function relating visual similarity to representational change in the hippocampus, whereby low levels of pairmate similarity were associated with no change, moderate levels of similarity were associated with differentiation, and the differentiation effect went away at higher levels of similarity.
evidence: This is a specific empirical finding from Wammes et al., 2022.
